headline: New law changes how much federal-backed financing Small Business Investment Companies can get and what counts as their private capital.
what_it_does: The law lowers the most SBA financing a Small Business Investment Company (SBIC) can have outstanding from 300% to 200% of its private capital, and raises the limit for groups of commonly controlled SBICs that pay interest quarterly or twice a year from $350 million to $475 million. Money an SBIC invests in rural areas, certain technology fields, or small manufacturers can be left out when figuring its limit, up to the lesser of $125 million or 50% of its private capital. It also lets SBICs count money from more government-sponsored corporations and from college or university trusts and endowments as private capital.

who_it_affects.how: Their maximum SBA financing is now tied to a lower multiple of private capital, with new exclusions for certain investments and broader sources counted as private capital.

who_it_affects.group: Small businesses in rural areas, certain technology fields, and small manufacturers
who_it_affects.how: SBIC investments in these businesses do not count toward the SBIC's financing limit, up to a cap.

who_it_affects.group: College and university trusts and endowments
who_it_affects.how: Money they invest in an SBIC can now count as that SBIC's private capital.
Funds from the business revenue of more of these corporations can now count as SBIC private capital.
The agency must apply the new financing limits and private capital rules when financing SBICs.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted May 19, 2026; the summary does not give a separate effective date.
